He could sneak into the top five rounds unless his commitment to Missouri scares teams off. Lohman works from 91-95 mph with his fastball and uses his 6-foot-4 build to create downhill plane. His over-the-top delivery enables him to stay on top of a low-80s slider that features two-plane depth at its best as well as a mid-70s curveball with similar shape. He has begun to use a low-80s splitter as a change of pace, and it along with his fastball and slider all could be solid offerings as he gains more strength and consistency. A short strider on the mound, Lohman has an upright delivery with a high release point. He doesn't have optimal shape on his fastball and slider, so he'll have to locate them well to succeed against more advanced hitters. He's an average athlete who provides a decent amount of strikes, and there's still plenty of projection remaining in his lanky frame.

O’Connor had an encouraging freshman year at Virginia but threw only 18 innings as a sophomore because of a lat injury. He made just eight relief outings in 2025, this time because of his elbow. A team willing to rehab him in house could be interested in the right-hander who has shown a fastball that sits 93-94 mph, touching 98 mph, along with a slider that flashes plus.

Jones has ranked as one of the best power hitters in the 2022 prep class and one of the top sluggers in the '24 and '25 college crops. He went undrafted as a Georgia high schooler and while sophomore-eligible last July because of concerns about his bat, athleticism and signability. After slugging 64 homers and winning two College World Series in three years at Louisiana State, he could land in the third or fourth round.The 6-foot-4, 246-pound Jones has plenty of strength and leverage in his right-handed stroke, generating top-of-the-scale raw power and exit velocities. He's doing a better job of understanding that he can hit the ball out of any park from foul pole to foul pole without selling out for home runs. Strikeouts always will be part of his game, but he's employing the opposite field more often and doing more damage against breaking balls. Jones has lost a little weight and is moving a little better as a junior, but he still has well-below-average speed and athleticism that hinder his value outside of the batter's box. While he does feature impressive arm strength, he's a limited defender who lacks range at first base and may wind up as a DH in pro ball. He caught in high school and briefly as a freshman, and he has seen sporadic action at third base as a junior, but neither position is a viable option.

After hitting .413 for the year and leading the PAC-12 in hitting in 2024, there were high hopes for Vu in his junior season. While he still had an OPS over 1.000 and stole 21 bases, it wasn’t quite as strong of a ‘25 campaign for the outfielder. He’s an aggressive and free swinger, and while he doesn’t swing and miss that much, especially on fastballs, or chase, his in-zone contact wasn’t as impressive. There is some thump coming from his max-effort swing, and he might best profile in center field with good speed, though he hasn’t played there at ASU.

Worley has better feel to spin than most pitchers in the high school class, topping 3,000 rpm with his low-80s slider while using a unique grip. He spent much of the spring working at 88-91 mph and peaking at 93 with his fastball, so it's unclear if teams will spend enough to lure him away from a Kennesaw State commitment. He displays some feel for a changeup but has inconsistent control.

Mayers can reach 102 mph with his fastball, though his lack of control makes him more of a project. After leading the Southland Conference in strikeouts in 2023 and 2024 at Nicholls State, he transferred to Louisiana State and whiffed 26 while walking 20 in 15 innings. His heater sits at 96-97 mph with carry and armside run, and he backs it up with an upper-80s slider, but he often misses the zone badly with both.

A 6-foot-4 lefty who spent his first three college seasons at Stony Brook in New York, redshirting in 2023, Book transferred to St. Joseph’s for his junior year and promptly earned Atlantic 10 Pitcher of the Year honors after finishing with a 3.53 ERA, 12.7 K/9 and 2.1 BB/9 rates and a .208 batting average against. He’s a pitchability left-hander who has a  86-90 mph fastball that plays up (32 percent miss rate), a 79-80 mph slider and some feel for a low-80s changeup.

After missing 2023 recovering from Tommy John surgery, Prager became the ace of Texas A&M's College World Series runner-up club last year. The Angels drafted him in the third round, but a hefty NIL package induced him to return to College Station for his redshirt junior season. His stuff and Draft stock took a downturn in 2025, when his fastball parked at 88 mph and his low-80s slider was less effective. His upper-70s changeup is his best pitch.

Gillespie pitched just 19 innings in two seasons at Georgia before transferring to UNC Charlotte, where he recorded a 2.42 ERA with 131 strikeouts (fourth in NCAA Division I) in 100 1/3 innings. He threw more sliders (798, 61 percent of his total pitches) and recorded more whiffs (99) with his slide piece than any pitcher in D-I. It's a 78-82 mph weapon and he can vary the break on it to get swing and misses in the zone or to elicit chases. He has a fringy 89-92 mph fastball and profiles as a reliever in pro ball.

McCutcheon homered just twice in his first two seasons at Missouri State, the second of which was cut short when he broke his right arm running into an outfield fence last March. He concentrated on adding strength during his recovery, and that has paid off with off with 15 homers and a .358/.444/.647 junior year. Data-driven teams will be attracted to his combination of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities, all of which are better than average. McCutcheon employs a leg kick yet usually is on time with his quick left-handed swing. His bat speed and ability to square up balls produces solid raw power, with most of his homers traveling to his pull side. He does damage against all types of pitches and lefties as well as righties, though his tendency to hit the ball on the ground may limit him to 15 homers per year with wood bats. While he can be slow out of the batter's box, McCutcheon has fringy to average speed once he gets going and shows some savvy on the bases. Counting summer leagues, he has played everywhere on the diamond but catcher, and he spent most of the last two seasons in left field after playing mostly second and third base as a freshman. More of a gritty than a smooth defender, he'll probably get another shot at second base in pro ball, with left field as his fallback position because he has fringy arm strength and range.

New Jersey's top prep position prospect in 2022, Martin turned down offers from pro clubs to stay home and play at Rutgers. He didn't see much action as a freshman with the Scarlet Knights, prompting a transfer to Georgia State in 2024, and he broke out this spring after another move to Kansas State. He slashed .320/.420/.612 with 14 homers while replacing 2024 Twins first-rounder Kaelen Culpepper at shortstop and also seeing action in center field. Martin's best tool is his plus raw power, which plays mostly to his pull side. His right-handed stroke features plenty of bat speed and leverage, producing high exit velocities. There are concerns about his frequency and quality of contact, however, because he has a swing-happy approach and struggles against non-fastballs. While Martin can display plus straight-line speed, he's more fringy to average out of the batter's box and isn't aggressive on the bases. He's an erratic defender with an average arm at shortstop, so he likely will move to second base or become a full-time outfielder in pro ball. He probably fits better on a corner than in center field at the next level.

After beginning his college journey at Seminole State College, Van Dyke spent the past two years pitching almost exclusively out of the Stetson bullpen, settling in as the Hatters’ closer in 2025 and racking up nine saves. He’s a strong reliever-only type, one who could be an intriguing senior sign with a fastball up to 97 mph and a low-80s slider, both of which miss bats.

After two years at Lower Columbia College, Stransky moved on to catch at Fresno State for two years and was a Buster Posey Collegiate Catcher of the Year semifinalist. He’s an excellent athlete behind the dish with a lean frame and long levers. He has good arm strength and speed while showing durability by catching nearly every game for the Bulldogs. He finished with double digits in home runs and stolen bases in 2025 while making a ton of contact (8.4 percent K rate) and walking more than he struck out, and he could be an intriguing senior sign.

The son of Brandon Lyon, who spent parts of 12 years in the big leagues, Isaac Lyon is an athletic right-hander who served as Grand Canyon’s Friday night starter this spring. He fills up the zone with a three-pitch mix that is more feel than pure stuff. He’ll touch 95 mph with his fastball, sitting 90-91, with a ton of two-seamer life to it. He has plus feel for a changeup he throws off of his fastball well and he’ll confidently throw it at any point. His hard 83-85 mph slider is an effective breaking ball.

Martin is a 6-foot-5 reliever who finished tied for fourth among all Division I pitchers with 14 saves in 2025. He has a heavy, sinking fastball that touches 97 mph that gets a ton of groundball outs and he does a nice job missing bats with an average 80-mph slider.

Boser spent three years at South Florida and was on Draft radars last year, landing on MLB Pipeline's Top 250 list after coming back from a broken hamate and continuing to show the kind of production he had the year prior as a sophomore. After playing well in the Cape Cod League, he moved from Tampa to Gainesville to play for the University of Florida and has put himself in position to be one of the higher-end senior signs of this Draft class. A strong, right-handed hitter, Boser has always shown a propensity for doing damage. There's strength and bat speed with good balance at the plate. There's also plenty of power for him to tap into, and he's shown the ability to drive the ball for extra bases and out of the park to all fields. Whether he can get to that pop at the next level is the question as he does swing and miss quite a good amount, and his miss rate did go up as the Gators got into conference play. Boser gets very high marks for his makeup, and he worked hard to improve his athleticism, running speed and defensive ability to make him a more viable all-around prospect. He has the ability to play three infield positions capably, and some think he's the best shortstop on the Gators, though he's played more third than anywhere else this season. A team taking him could send him out at short, but he could develop into a regular at the hot corner or second, with a floor as a productive super-utility type.

Spencer was the closer for a 2023 Indiana State team that made an unexpected run to the NCAA super regionals, though he injured his shoulder in his final outing of the season. He avoided surgery but didn't pitch that summer or fall, then started slowly as a junior season before moving into the Sycamores rotation at midseason. He turned down the Phillies as a 14th-rounder last July to transfer to Texas, where he emerged as the best college senior in the 2025 Draft before injuring his shoulder in April and undergoing season-ending surgery. Spencer added 2 mph to his fastball this spring, sitting at 93-96 mph, touching 98 and maintaining his velocity deep into games, albeit with more downhill angle than carry or run. His sweeping slider always has been his best pitch and it became a wipeout offering after it picked up 5 mph compared to a year ago, averaging 88 mph and reaching 91. He barely threw a changeup at Indiana State but now has the makings of a solid mid-80s cambio with depth. Not only did Spencer improve his velocity and shapes under the tutelage of famed Longhorns pitching coach Max Weiner, but he also gained better mechanics. His delivery is still funky in the back and features some effort, but he was more direct to the plate and more on top of his offerings before he got hurt. His surgery clouds his Draft status, but he was a three-pitch starter working his way toward the first round until his shoulder gave out.

After missing his 2024 Mississippi high school senior season recovering from Tommy John surgery, Johnson set a Pearl River record with 12 wins this spring while fashioning a 2.28 ERA with 70 strikeouts in 71 innings. He works with a 90-93 mph that touches 96 and a low-80s slider, getting down the mound well and creating deception with extension and a low arm slot. He'll transfer to Auburn as a sophomore if he doesn't turn pro.

The best position prospect among south Texas high schoolers in 2022, Flores went undrafted because he wanted to attend Texas and learn from five-time All-Star Troy Tulowitzki. He struggled offensively and defensively after Tulowitzki left the coaching staff before his freshman year but has thrived the last two seasons after Tulowitzki returned. After his commitment to the Longhorns once again left him unpicked as one of the top sophomore-eligibles in 2024, he led the team in extra-base hits for the second straight season but slumped horribly in the final two months. An aggressive right-handed hitter, Flores looks to launch balls in the air to his pull side and has the bat speed, strength and leverage to generate 20 homers per season. He's equally effective against lefties and righties, though his free-swinging ways make him unlikely to hit for a high average or draw many walks. He has some of the highest chase rates in college baseball against curveballs and sliders but makes consistent contact when he swings at strikes. Scouts have mixed opinions about Flores' long-term ability to remain at shortstop. He has below-average speed yet fluid actions, and his quick hands and plus arm strength help him make plays. If he winds up moving, he has the tools to become at least a solid defender at third base and the power to profile there.

In 2020, Mick Abel was the No. 15 overall pick in the Draft out of the Oregon high school ranks. Three years later, Noble Meyer came out of the same school, Jesuit High School, and landed No. 10 overall. Anyone who saw Hamilton, who attends Sam Barlow High School, pitch at Perfect Game National last summer might have thought he would give the Beaver State a third prep pitching first-rounder, though he didn't throw as well at the Area Code Games later on and was forced to the sidelines with right elbow discomfort ahead of his first start back in March. Scouts were a little disappointed Hamilton didn't throw more this fall, but he showed enough over the summer to whet their appetites, though they were waiting to see him on the mound as the calendar turned to May. Similar to predecessors Abel and Meyer, Hamilton is long, lean and projectable. He's already up to 95-96 mph with his fastball with good carry and some tailing action, and it's easy to envision more consistent velocity coming as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. When he's on top of his slider, it's a tight breaking ball with traditional two-plane break, getting a lot of swings-and-misses. He has good feel for his changeup, especially for a high schooler. Fairly athletic on the mound, Hamilton throws all three of his pitches without a ton of effort and should gain even more consistency with his command as he matures, even if those Oregonian first-rounders have struggled with command in the professional ranks. Hamilton switched his college commitment from Oregon State to LSU this fall, and with the injury keeping him from being scouted this spring, he could end up heading to Baton Rouge.

Haley is both one of the most talented prep left-handers and one of the best human-interest stories in the 2025 Draft. He had Tommy John surgery on his left elbow before his high school career began, though he learned to throw right-handed so he could play while rehabbing. He was diagnosed with non-Hodgkins lymphoma after recovering from his elbow reconstruction and continued to play while undergoing chemotherapy and radiation treatments. He was pronounced cancer-free in December 2022 but suffered another tear in the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow last spring, requiring internal brace surgery that truncated his junior season and kept him off the showcase circuit. Largely unknown before he attended the Super 60 Showcase in February, Haley opened eyes by working with a 91-94 mph fastball with carry and armside run, and he has maintained that velocity while topping out at 97 as a senior. He has a hammer low-80s curveball, as well as a solid slider with a bit more power, though it sometimes blends into and detracts from his curve. He also shows the ability to kill spin on a low-80s changeup but hasn't needed to utilize it much. Haley comes from an athletic family that includes a father (Jimmy) who played in the Canadian Football League, a mother (Shelley) who played college basketball at West Virginia Wesleyan and a brother (Gage) who pitches at Arkansas-Little Rock. Talon moves down the mound well, creating plenty of extension and provides strikes with a clean delivery that has a bit of a head dunk. Teams aren't sure how they should treat his medical history and lack of track record, so he could wind up at Vanderbilt, where he'd be a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2027.

Moore had some success pitching almost exclusively out of the bullpen in his first two years at Old Dominion. He had scouts excited about what his junior year might look like when he was up to 97 mph with his fastball last fall and given a chance to start full-time. The results were mixed as his stuff and command regressed when asked to stretch out as part of the Monarchs rotation, though he still provides some intriguing traits from a left-hander. At 6-foot-4, Moore has size and some projection on his side. While he's shown more premium velocity in shorter stints and topped out at 97 mph this spring, his heater fluctuated throughout the year and he averaged around 92 mph with the pitch. During his mound session at the Draft Combine, he averaged 93.7 mph with his fastball, throwing it with good sink. He has good feel to spin his low-80s slider and can miss bats with it, though he's landed it for strikes and got more swing-and-miss with it as a reliever in the past. He's worked on a low-80s changeup, but it's clearly behind the other two offerings. Teams that believe Moore can develop a true three-pitch mix might give him the chance to start out of the gate to see if he can find more consistency. But given the issues he had with maintaining his stuff and the regression in his command when he was in Old Dominion's rotation, it might be better for him to head back to the bullpen, where his sinker-slider combination could tick back up.

Bullard raised his stock more than any high school position prospect in Texas this spring. Teams have differing opinions about his offensive upside, but enough clubs like him that he could fit in the top three rounds if he's signable. He has a strong commitment to Texas A&M and could wind up in College Station. Scouts who believe in Bullard like his bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate. Others have questions about his hitting ability and worry that he hasn't faced much in the way of quality competition. He employs more of a gap-to-gap approach right now and makes a lot of groundball contact, but he also has bat speed and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame that could translate into 15 homers per season as he continues to get stronger. Bullard owns plus speed and knows how to use it on the bases and in the outfield. He displays good instincts in center field and should be able to remain there in college or pro ball. He has average arm strength and could handle all three outfield spots if needed.

Smith entered the year as a potential second-round pick, but a rough spring (5.23 ERA, albeit with 58 strikeouts in 41 1/3 innings) dinged his stock. He lost velocity and trust in his fastball, which topped out at 93 mph after reaching 96 in the past, and became overly dependent on his plus mid-80s sweeper. At his best, he's a four-pitch starter who provides strikes.

Jay has been a constant force in Dallas Baptist's lineup since he arrived in 2023, launching 61 homers and slugging .696 in three seasons to become the Patriots' all-time leader in both categories. There are concerns about his ability to make consistent contact and remain a catcher, but his power, arm strength and athleticism for the position will get him taken in the top five rounds. He's the grandson of Joey Jay, a two-time All-Star who pitched 13 seasons in the big leagues. His combination of bat speed and strength gives Jay at least plus-plus raw power that plays to all fields and produces higher exit velocities than most college players. But instead of letting his pop play naturally, he sells out for home runs with an uphill right-handed swing and overly aggressive approach. He has cut his strikeout rate from 31 percent in his first two college seasons to 25 percent this spring, but he still swings-and-misses at pitches in the zone far too frequently. He looked overmatched with wood bats in the Cape Cod League last summer as well. Jay has average speed once he gets going and can pick his spots to steal, swiping 29 bases in 32 attempts (91 percent) during his college career. He shows solid arm strength behind the plate but is a below-average receiver and blocker who struggles to handle live-armed but erratic teammate James Ellwanger. He moves and throws well enough to make left field a possibility, and Dallas Baptist has deployed him there at times this year.

Underwood rarely touched 90 mph with his fastball last summer and looked like a projectable high school left-hander who would need to develop in college before he was ready for pro ball. Now that he has begun to add strength and velocity as a senior, he could get drafted high enough to divert him from a commitment to Georgia Tech. He possesses some of the best feel for spin in this year's prep class. Underwood has averaged 90 mph with his fastball this spring and topped out at 93 with carry and armside run, and he still has room to add plenty more muscle to his 6-foot-2 frame. There's some debate as to which of his high-spin breaking balls is better, with his upper-70s downer curveball a tick more reliable than his tighter and slightly harder slider. His 82-85 mph changeup features promising fade but is a bit firm. Underwood uses his athleticism to repeat his efficient delivery well. He shows aptitude for throwing strikes and mixing four pitches, all of which he trusts. If he continues to get stronger and better, he might become a No. 3 or 4 starter one day.

Woolfolk snuck onto the back end of MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 Draft prospects in 2024 but went undrafted, partially because of a knee injury that forced him from his College World Series start. He spent all of ‘25 in Virginia’s rotation, with uneven results, but still missed bats with a fastball up to 96 mph, a mid-80s power slider and a changeup thrown around the same velocity that can be effective at times. He did his best work in college when closing for the Cavaliers back in ‘23, so a team could take him as top-10-round money saver and put him in the bullpen to allow him to move more quickly through a system.

In 2025, Penn State's baseball program was the beneficiary of a pair of players coming from St. Joseph's. Ryan Weingartner was the Nittany Lions' shortstop and DeSanto was a mainstay in the rotation after two years of starting for the Hawks and a strong turn in the Cape Cod League, when he was named Harwich's Pitcher of the Year. The big left-hander wasn't quite as effective with Penn State, but he did take over as the Friday night guy in March. From a pure stuff standpoint, the 6-foot-4 DeSanto isn't anything to write home about. It's a below-average fastball from a velocity standpoint, averaging only around 88 mph in 2025 and topping out at 93 mph. But the data on the pitch is off the charts, with huge spin rates that lead to a ton of carry to make it very effective above the hands, a reason why it produced a 24-percent miss rate and opponents only hit .182 against the pitch. His upper-70s slider also features good spin, and he kills it with a changeup thrown a tick or two harder than the breaking ball. In addition to the metrics, DeSanto's funky delivery adds a ton of deception, allowing all of his stuff to play up. There's not a ton of margin for error here based on the velocity profile -- perhaps a team will think a few more ticks out of that big frame are possible -- and he'll have to find better command, especially of his breaking stuff, for him to be a back-end starter at the highest level.

Galvan went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible a year ago but should fit in the first five rounds this July as one of the better options in a shallow pool of college catchers. He has improved on both sides of the ball this spring, giving him a ceiling of a big league starter and a floor of a reserve who can get the job done defensively while providing some power. How well he hits will determine which end of the spectrum he winds up on. Galvan offers plus raw power that plays to all fields but comes with questions about how much he'll be able to tap into it against pro pitching. A right-handed hitter, he has significantly improved his swing decisions in 2025 but comes up empty too often on pitches in the strike zone. He can get too pull-happy and struggles to make contact against non-fastballs. Using a one-knee setup, Galvan has cleaned up his receiving and blocking and now provides average defense behind the plate. His solid arm strength, quick transfer and throwing accuracy shut down the running game, and opponents rarely have tested him this spring. Scouts praise his leadership skills and ability to run a pitching staff.

Mitchell comes from a football family that includes an uncle (Keithen McCant) who quarterbacked in the Canadian Football League and an older brother (Richard Morrison) who played wide receiver at the University of Arizona. But Mitchell has been pointed toward a baseball future since he was a youngster and entered 2025 as one of the best high school left-handers in the Draft after pitching for the U.S. 18-and-under national team last summer. He performed well during the first month of his senior season but missed the rest of the spring with shoulder fatigue. Mitchell's fastball sits at 90-92 mph and tops out at 94, playing better than its velocity because he hides it well and it carries past barrels at the top of the strike zone. He displays fine aptitude for throwing an upper-70s curveball with depth that works well in tandem with the shape of his heater. He has begun dabbling with a low-80s changeup that fades and sinks, though he doesn't use it much. His ability to repeat his athletic three-quarters delivery allows Mitchell to provide consistent strikes. His slender 6-foot-3 frame has plenty of room to add muscle, which could add power to his fastball and curveball and make both of them plus offerings. It's unclear how his shoulder woes will affect his Draft status, and he'll pitch at Texas if he attends college.

At 6-foot-5, Lauridsen is the prototypical projectable high school right-hander. He’s very athletic on the mound and gets high marks for his makeup, not to mention what his future stuff could be. He’s committed to Southern Cal for college, but teams could bite on his upside to sign him away from school, thanks to a sinking fastball that touches 95-96 mph and the potential to have a very good changeup and two distinct breaking pitches.

Porco, who stands 6-foot-8, can throw really hard, while not always knowing where it’s going (8.8 BB/9 in his college career). The West Virginia right-hander has been up to 97-98 mph with his fastball at times, then dialed it back when given a chance to start, with minimal benefit, and he landed back in the bullpen, which should be his future home. He throws an 86-90 mph cutter and 88-89 mph changeup to back up the heater.

Heyman was eligible last year but went undrafted after a rough spring with the Gators. He bounced back this year, cutting down on his swing-and-miss some to end up with a .975 OPS. There’s some power potential, with 29 homers combined in 2024 and ‘25 from the right side of the plate. He has the chance to stick behind the dish defensively with solid defensive skills and a strong arm.

A redshirt sophomore, Brock slashed .462/.565/.870 and ranked third among national junior college players in hiting, on-base percentage and OPS (1.435) and fourth in slugging. He also was the only 20-20 player at that level, going deep 20 times and swiping 27 bases. He has plus-plus speed, rare for a catcher, and may be able to stay behind the plate. If he can't, he's quick enough to handle center field. He'll transfer to Oklahoma if he doesn't turn pro.

One of the better hitters hailing from the junior college ranks, Vanek did nothing but hit over two years at Chipola, including finishing with a .395 average this past spring. It’s a hit-over-power approach with a clean swing and good strike zone awareness. Some question his impact while others think there’s power to come as he matures. He’s a better athlete than some give him credit for, with the chance to handle the outfield corners rather than be locked in at first base, where he played during his time in the Draft League this summer. He’ll head to Florida State if the Draft doesn’t go his way.

Scouts were excited to see what Smith might do on the mound at Memphis after he played his first two college seasons at Northwest Mississippi CC, but the two-way player worked just five innings before breaking his leg in an outfield collision in early April. Athletic and projectable at 6-foot-5 and 185 pounds, he sat at 93-95 mph and touched 99 with good metrics on his fastball before he got hurt. He also can spin some interesting mid-80s sliders, but he's still raw on the mound and will need time to develop.

The son of three-time All-Star Sean Casey, Jake bounced back from a .216/.323/.523 junior season and Tommy John surgery in 2024 to slash .356/.500/.736 with 17 homers and 20 steals this spring. He has a smooth left-handed swing -- not surprising considering his dad -- and shows the ability to loft the ball in the air to his pull side. He has solid speed and enough arm strength to play right field.

Bravo spent his first season at Texas Tech as a little-used two-way player, getting 30 at-bats as an outfielder and 7 1/3 innings as a reliever. He blossomed as a full-time hitter in 2024, winning the Big 12 Conference batting championship at .378. He didn't defend that title this spring but continued to make consistent contact while improving his power and basestealing ability. A right-handed hitter, Bravo smokes hard-hit line drives to all fields. He's doing a better job of lifting balls in the air as a junior, showing more pull power and the potential for 15 homers per season. He'd be more effective at the plate if he made better swing decisions as his aggression undermines his bat-to-ball skills and cuts into his walk totals. Bravo has looked a bit quicker this year, flashing solid speed at times and making things happen on the bases more often. After splitting time between left and center field last season, he has moved to right and exhibited fine range and plus arm strength, no surprise considering his fastball reached 93 mph as a freshman. He also played some second base during fall practice and briefly this spring.

King is all about speed and defense. His .291 average at West Virginia in 2025 was a career high, and he walked as much as he struck out. There isn’t a ton of impact, and while he’ll show some raw power in batting practice, he focused more on shooting line drives to the gaps this spring and ended up hitting in the leadoff spot. He also can really defend in center field and has speed that could be an asset on the basepaths as well.

In his fourth season at Stanford, Haskins found his power stroke, elevating to his pull side for 14 homers while hitting .326. He moved from shortstop to third and looked comfortable at the hot corner, using his better-than-average arm strength and accuracy effectively. He’s a solid senior sign option who has the chance to be a utility option as a pro.

Chrest got off to a good start in his first year at Florida State following two years at Jacksonville, with a 2.70 ERA over his first four starts as the Seminoles’ midweek starter, but an elbow injury shelved him for the rest of the year. Though a bit undersized at six-foot, some scouts give him the chance to start because of his arm strength and solid delivery. He’s a strike-thrower with a potential four-pitch mix, a low-90s fastball complemented best by a mid-80s changeup, though he has a slider and cutter as well.

Ware intrigued scouts for two seasons at Pearl River (Miss.) CC but he pitched just 32 innings, missing time in 2023 with back issues and last spring with a tired arm. He went undrafted both years, transferred to Louisiana State and claimed a spot in the weekend rotation with a strong fall -- but he worked just 21 1/3 innings as his stuff and control regressed. At his best, he has a 92-94 mph fastball that reached 96 with impressive carry and an upper-70s downer curveball that tops 3,000 rpm. His older brother Bryson set an Auburn record with 24 homers in 2023 before signing with the Phillies as an eighth-rounder.

After four years at Division III Misericorida in Pennsylvania, Lanzendorfer spent his fifth collegiate season at the University of Virginia and served as an effective left-handed reliever who finished with five saves, a 2.90 ERA, 11.6 K/9 and .195 BAA. He finds the zone enough with a 90-94 mph fastball that plays up because of life up in the zone and deception and has a fringy low-80s slider. He could be an interesting money-saving senior sign.

After two years at Texas Tech, Harrelson transferred to Florida State for his junior year and had a fine campaign with the Seminoles, finishing with a .339/.444/.462 line and 15 steals. He’s a left-handed hitter with a slasher-type approach at the plate. He provides limited power, but he makes a ton of contact and can spray it around the field. He’s a plus runner who could get the chance to play center field at the next level.

Grossman is a native of Hawaii who began his college career at the University of Utah but moved to Salt Lake Community College after barely seeing any mound time as a freshman. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has plenty of arm strength with a fastball up to 97 mph, and he can miss bats with a low-80s slider, but his scattered command could eventually land him in a bullpen.

A native of Charleston, South Carolina, Franklin headed south to play for TNXL Academy in Florida. He’s a high-energy player who has a strong right-handed swing. There’s some feel to hit, but it’s a bit of a power-over-hit approach. His bat is ahead of his defense, but he has a chance to stick behind the plate. He’s committed to head back home to the University of South Carolina for college.

After a four-year varsity career playing for former big leaguer Matt Diaz at Lakeland High School in Florida, Donay headed a bit north to start his career at Virginia Tech. He started establishing his power hitting bona fides with a dozen homers in 39 games there, but then came back to his home state to suit up for the Gators in 2024 and 2025. He hit 32 more home runs combined and finished his junior season with an OPS over 1.000, though questions about his swing and his defensive future lingered. Donay's calling card was, is and always will be his prodigious raw power from the right side of the plate. He's a towering presence in the box at 6-foot-5 and when he makes contact, he can launch the ball a long way, and he is fully capable of hitting the ball out to all fields. The big question is if he can make enough contact to get to that power. Donay owns a career 30.9 percent strikeout rate, and while he did cut that to 25.2 percent this spring while upping his walk rate, the holes in his swing are still concerning. There are some who feel that Donay has a chance to catch at the next level, and he has easily plus arm strength as a big asset. But others think his size and lack of agility will be obstacles too large to overcome. He has seen time at first base and in right field at various spots, should a team decide to move his power potential out from behind the dish.

Smith is a big-bodied first base/DH type with plus raw power. There are swing-and-miss concerns he’ll have to address once he gets to the pro game, but his ability to drive the ball to all fields could be interesting in the later rounds. He’s a below average defender.

Horn drew comparisons to Bubba Chandler as a Georgia high school right-hander/quarterback in 2022, and while evaluators rated Chandler (now the best mound prospect in the Minors) as having more explosive stuff, Horn was a superior athlete, strike thrower and passer. A four-star football recruit, he turned down seven-figure overtures from MLB teams to attend Missouri as a two-sport athlete. He wowed scouts in his college baseball debut in February 2023 but injured his elbow in his second outing and eventually had Tommy John surgery that cost him all of 2024. Returning to the mound this April following spring football, Horn struck out 14 in 10 2/3 innings while working at 93-95 mph and touching 98 with armside run and sink on his fastball. He hasn't recaptured feel for his slider, though he did show the ability to get chases with his 82-86 mph sweeper. He barely used his mid-80s changeup with fade. Horn creates quality extension with his 6-foot-4 frame and athletic delivery, providing deception with a low arm slot and release height. He's still refining his control and command after working just 15 innings in three college seasons, but they should become average as he gains more experience. Clubs are trying to weigh his upside versus his lack of track record, and his desire to turn pro in baseball while continuing to compete for Missouri's starting quarterback job complicates matters.

Smith spent two years at the JUCO level, pitching at Indian River State College in Florida before heading on to Central Florida for his junior season. He didn’t get a ton of innings (28 2/3), but used them well, finishing with a 2.83 ERA and 2.2 BB/9. There could be more to unlock here with more mound reps, with some scouts thinking he has the chance to start because he has a fastball up to 96 mph that he commands well to go along with an effective cutter, changeup and slider.

picks.blurb: Moore may be the best Illinois high school hitter since Alek Thomas went in the second round of the 2018 Draft. He made hard contact everywhere he went on showcase circuit last summer, including batting .357 without a strikeout in 16 plate appearances in the Area Code Games. He has had a puzzling spring, showing improved strength but regressing in all phases of the game. A switch-hitter, Moore features a compact swing and smacks line drives all over the field, stroking the ball with more authority from the left side of the plate. His combination of hitting ability, bat speed and strength should produce 15-20 homers annually once he adds some more loft to his stroke. He has the aptitude to work counts and hit the ball where it's pitched, but he hasn't barreled balls as expected during his senior season. Moore's speed grades range from average to solid and he shows good instincts on the bases. The Tennessee recruit is athletic and has reliable hands, but he lacks premium range and his fringy arm strength almost certainly will push him to second base in the future. Besides his physical ability, he also earns praise for his intelligence and competitiveness.

Driessen has worked out of the bullpen in all three of his seasons with the Jackrabbits and enjoyed his best campaign yet this spring, finishing with a 4.37 ERA and 50 strikeouts in 35 innings. The top prospect in the Dakotas, he works with a 91-96 mph fastball and has a high-spin curveball that sits around 80 mph, though he needs to improve his control and command.

After appearing in 16 games, all but one in relief, as a Virginia Tech freshman, Stieg moved into the Hokies' rotation as a sophomore in 2024. He showed enough glimpses of now stuff and upside serving as the team's Sunday starter to generate buzz for an exciting Draft year in 2025. That never came to pass as he needed Tommy John surgery at the end of his sophomore season and didn't throw a pitch this year. There are many attributes the 6-foot-4 Stieg can bring to a professional organization once he's healthy. It all starts with a two-seam sinking fastball that has extreme run to it. In 2024, it averaged 93.5 mph and topped out at 97 mph, and while it didn't miss many bats, it did get groundball contact. He complements it with a solid low-80s slider that can miss bats and an effective changeup thrown around the same velocity that serves as a swing-and-miss pitch as well and gets weak contact on the ground. Stieg delivers all of his offerings from a three-quarter slot and did a fine job of throwing his arsenal for strikes in 2024. He has the makings of a back-end starter if he can build off his sophomore campaign, though the lack of track record -- he's thrown just 70 1/3 college innings in his career -- could make some teams pause. A team could send him out as a starter, but he could eventually find his way to the bullpen, where his sinker-slider combination could tick up.

A 6-foot-5 projectable right-hander from the southern California ranks, Boles has shown a fastball up to 94 mph in the past, though he mostly pitched at around 90 mph this spring. He has a high-spin low-80s slider than can be plus when he harnesses it, though that happens inconsistently. He’s committed to Texas if the Draft doesn’t go his way.

Weyrich could be an interesting money-saving senior sign after saving 12 games over the past two seasons as Marshall’s closer. The Appy League alum is a near-submariner with a funky fastball look, usually sitting 87-89 mph, but sometimes up to 93 mph, so there could be more consistent velocity in the tank. He has a mid-70s slider as well, but he almost never throws it, going almost exclusively with his hard to square up heater.

Puyallup High School in the state of Washington has had seven players drafted, and while it's been a participant in the National High School Invitational twice, it hasn't had a player selected since 2015, the same year of its first NHSI appearance. Pike was part of the team that came back to the USA Baseball event in 2024 and he's continued to attract attention on both sides of the ball, participating in summer showcase events like the Area Code Games and MLB's High School All-American Game. At the plate, Pike is a switch-hitter with some present strength and a fair share of raw power. He has good rhythm at the plate, but his timing is often off as he is prone to guessing too much to try to get to his power. He has the ability to get to it naturally and there are those who feel once he trusts that, some of the timing issues could be corrected and he'd be able to cut down on the swing-and-miss. He probably lacks the footspeed to play shortstop, so a move to second or third, where his plus arm would play well, is likely. On the mound, Pike was up to 96-97 mph in shorter showcase stints over the summer, and came out of the gate this spring up to 95 mph with his fastball. He's more thrower than pitcher and his velocity can drop as he gets deeper into outings. He throws a solid changeup with fade, selling it with good arm speed, but not everyone likes his slider, as he is prone to get underneath it. He's headed to Oregon State, where he could get the chance to play both ways, should the Draft not work out.

David Upchurch played defensive tackle at West Virginia and signed as an undrafted free agent with the Steelers, though he never played in the NFL. His son, Myles, also played football at St. Albans School in Washington, D.C., but his future is on the diamond as a right-handed pitcher. After showing off his stuff at summer showcase events like the East Coast Professional Showcase and Area Code Games, he's had a bit of an up-and-down senior season, though his size and stuff are still intriguing. At 6-foot-4 and 215 pounds, Upchurch offers size and arm strength to any team interested in the prep right-hander. He can run his fastball up to 95-96 mph, but typically sits around 91-93, and there have been some questions about the life of his heater. His best secondary offering is a low-80s slider that can flash above-average, though not consistently. Some scouts have seen a separate, slower upper-70s curve, but others have only seen a slider. The two might run into each other, and with his arm slot, focusing on a slider only might be the smart move. He did show some feel for a changeup over the summer but has largely ditched it this spring. Upchurch can tilt to his glove side on his delivery at times, which can lead to the appearance of a higher arm slot. He also doesn't always repeat his motion, leading to spotty command. His strength and athleticism should be assets going forward, and believers that think there's more to unlock as he focuses on his craft could be interested in signing him away from his commitment to Alabama.

Barnett is a physical 6-foot-5, 210-pounder who stands out with his power potential and exit velocities while also showing off a strong arm and playing a quality third base. He does come with some swing-and-miss concerns and some evaluators wonder if he might have more upside on the mound. There's chatter that a team or two may be willing to spend heavily to lure him away from his Alabama commitment.

Illinois has spawned four high school pitchers who signed for first-round money in the last three Drafts -- Owen Murphy, Noah Schultz, Blake Wolters, Ryan Sloan -- and has another possibility for 2025. Appenzeller is one of the more projectable left-handers available and has a higher ceiling at the same stage than fellow Glenwood HS (Chatham) product Reid Detmers, who became a first-rounder after three years at Louisville. His stuff took a step forward in 2024 and teams believe he has much more left in his tank, though his late start this spring after playing basketball has limited the ability to evaluate him. Appenzeller boosted his fastball from the mid-80s as a sophomore to the upper 80s as a junior to the low 90s last summer, topping out at 94 mph, but then operated at 84-89 this spring. He can generate carry on a four-seamer and armside run and sink on a two-seamer. He gets plenty of horizontal action on an upper-70s slider, and his low-80s changeup fades in the opposite direction. Appenzeller still has plenty of room to put weight on his athletic 6-foot-6 frame, which should add more power to his fastball and slider and create more separation between his heater and changeup. The Tennessee recruit repeats his delivery well, filling the strike zone from a low, wide arm angle that is tough on left-handed hitters. He combines stuff and savvy and also draws praise for his mound presence.

While his twin brother JoJo has surpassed him as a prospect this spring, rocketing into the first round, Jacob is more physical and could go in the second or third round to a team that believes in his bat. Some scouts think he'll make enough contact to tap into his well-above-average raw power, while others have swing-and-miss concerns. The siblings will play together at Mississippi State if they attend college, though that's unlikely. Parker packs plenty of strength in his 6-foot-3, 215-pound frame and puts on one of the best batting-practice shows in the high school class. He produces high exit velocities when he makes contact. He can mishit balls out of the park and is at his best when he lets his all-fields power come naturally. But his left-handed swing gets too long and uphill, and he gets too pull-happy when he hunts home runs, leading to strikeouts, and he hasn't faced much quality competition or had much success when he has. Parker moves very well for his size, displaying plus straight-line speed and more solid quickness on the bases. He has pushed his fastball to 90 mph when pitching, and that arm strength adds to his right-field profile. He could be a solid defender on the corners and could get the chance to show what he can do in center field at the next level.

Wood is a 6-foot-2 right-hander with an old-school delivery that includes a big rock and fully closed front side. He can change arm angles and release points to add to his deception with a fastball that typically sits in the 88-92 mph range with run and sink, topping out at 95. The Arizona recruit has natural feel to spin a slurvy breaking ball and also works with a changeup.

After redshirting his freshman year, Brown settled in as Sacramento State’s closer, finishing tied for fourth among Division I pitchers with 14 saves in 2025. He’s a 6-foot-6 right-hander with a fastball that works in the 89-91 mph range, and he backs it up with an average slider and splitter.

Early in his high school career, Peeples emerged as one of the top outfielders in the 2025 prep class. He looks the part with a pretty left-handed swing and a frame that resembles that of a young Christian Yelich, though his struggles on the showcase circuit last summer have clubs wondering if they can draft him early enough to lure him away from a Georgia commitment. With Peeples' combination of bat speed and projectable strength, as well as a stroke designed to drive balls in the air to his pull side, he could grow into 25-homer power or more. To get there, he'll have to improve his timing at the plate after having swing-and-miss issues against all types of pitching last summer. He has a big leg kick and gets overly aggressive rather than allowing his pop to come naturally. Peeples' instincts allow him to play a little quicker than his fringy speed on the bases and in the outfield. Nevertheless, he won't be a basestealing threat and almost certainly will have to move from center field to a corner in pro ball. His arm stands out more for its accuracy than its average arm strength.

When thinking about left-handed pitchers to come out of Long Island, the first thought might be of Frank Viola, who wouldn't sign out of high school and went on to become a second-round pick out of St. John's in 1981. A bit more recently, there was Steven Matz, a Mets second-round pick in 2009 who signed and has spent parts of 11 seasons in the big leagues. He's the last prep southpaw from the area of New York to hit the big leagues, though Frusco is hoping to join him after showing off his wares at summer showcase events, then continuing to get exposure in MLB's Draft League and Draft Combine High School Game. If you like projectable lefties, then Frusco might be the prospect for you. At 6-foot-4 and 208 pounds, it's easy to dream on more physicality and a lot more velocity. Right now, his fastball velocity is below-average, typically sitting in the upper-80s, though he was getting to 91-92 mph at the Combine and in the Draft League. It's an invisible heater that gets a lot more swings and misses than it should thanks to its life and the deception in Frusco's delivery. He also has good feel to spin an 80-82 mph slider, and while he doesn't throw it much, there's a solid changeup in his future arsenal. Frusco will need to improve his command at the next level, but added strength to that frame will not only add mph to his heater, it should help him repeat his delivery and find the zone more consistently. If the Draft doesn't work out, it's easy to see him becoming a big-time 2028 Draft prospect after three years at Clemson.

California's Corona High School gets a lot of attention as one of the best prep baseball programs in the country, one that won USA Baseball's National High School Invitational in 2024 and made it to the semifinal this year. The trio of Seth Hernandez, Billy Carlson and Brady Ebel have understandably received most of the Draft buzz attention, but teams aren't sleeping on Bingaman, an impressive two-way player who has scouts that advocate for him both on the mound and at the plate. It might be a split camp, but it seems that the industry leans slightly in the direction of Bingaman, the 6-foot-1 right-hander. Strong, athletic and aggressive on the mound, he attacks hitters mostly with a two-pitch mix. His fastball sits around 92 mph more often than not, topping out at 95, and he misses a lot of bats with it because of its ride up in the zone and the fact that it's thrown with high spin and from a high overhand slot. He couples it with a hard curve that has good depth. There's a little feel for a changeup, but he doesn't use it much. Those who have concerns about him on the mound think there could be some reliever risk. Those who like him at the plate see a balanced, centered stance with the intent to do damage and a lot of raw power. Some see holes in the swing and that he can be pitched to effectively, and it's a little unclear where his home might be defensively. He plays right field for Corona, but he believes he can play third, currently manned by Ebel. If the Draft doesn't work out, he could go on to play both ways at Auburn.

Few players showed more improvement on the showcase circuit from 2023 to 2024 than Schaefer, and he keeps getting better. He capped his offseason with a strong performance at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship, helping him to continue to climb Draft boards. Despite being hampered by a hamstring injury this spring, he still could fit into the top three rounds. Schaefer has refined his right-handed swing while continuing to add bat speed and muscle to his lean 6-foot-3 frame. As he continues to mature physically and develop as a hitter, he could grow into 25-homer power that plays to all fields. He has a good eye at the plate but tends to get out in front of breaking pitches, so he'll need to make adjustments. A good athlete for his size, Schaefer possesses average speed and fine instincts on the bases. The Arkansas recruit has good actions and solid arm strength at shortstop, where he's a sound if not flashy defender. He'll probably slow a bit as he continues to gain strength, so most evaluators project that he'll wind up at third base.

A strong, 6-foot-3 super-compeititve right-hander who is committed to Oklahoma, Neckar features a lively fastball up to 96 mph and has shown the ability to maintain his velocity deep into starts. He backs it up with a high-spin curve that has some bite and depth to it, though he can scatter both at times out of the zone.
